info.title: Configuring and managing software RAID via mdadm

topic.para: MD-RAID is the native Linux software RAID stack handled directly by the kernel's md module.

Multiple Devices RAID (MD-RAID) is Linux’s native, kernel-level software RAID framework, designed to combine multiple physical drives into a single redundant logical volume without relying on proprietary hardware controllers or BIOS-based FakeRAID. Operating directly within the Linux block layer, it supports RAID levels 0, 1, 4, 5, 6, and 10, with management handled primarily through the mdadm utility. It features automatic boot-time array assembly, live status tracking via /proc/mdstat , background parity scrubbing, online capacity expansion, and hot-swaps for failed drives. Because it is hardware-agnostic and fully portable across Linux installations, MD-RAID remains the industry standard for flexible, vendor-independent storage redundancy.

listitem.para: mdadm: The main command-line utility used to create, assemble, build, manage, monitor, and repair pure Linux software RAID arrays (RAID 0, 1, 4, 5, 6, 10).
mdmon: A background daemon bundled with mdadm that monitors arrays using external metadata formats.
raid6check: A diagnostic tool included with mdadm packages used to verify and repair parity consistency on RAID 6 sets.
/proc/mdstat: A virtual system file used to instantly check real-time status, synchronization progress, and health of active MD arrays.

section.title: Naming software RAID devices
section.para: Adopting a clear naming convention for software RAID arrays is essential for efficient system administration. Incorporating the array's purpose or RAID level directly into its name allows for quick volume identification and prevents costly mistakes during routine maintenance.

section.title: Default names
section.para: By default, software RAID devices have names following the pattern mdN, where N is a number. For example, they can be accessed as /dev/md127 and are listed as md127 in /proc/mdstat and /proc/partitions.

section.title: Providing non-default names
section.para: As working with the default names might be clumsy, there are two ways how to work around this:

listitem.para: You can optionally specify a name for the RAID device when creating it with &yast; or on the command line with mdadm --create '/dev/md/ NAME'. The device name will still be mdN, but the link /dev/md/NAME will be created:
The device will still be listed as md127 under /proc.

This will cause names like myRAID to be used as a real device name. The device will not only be accessible at /dev/myRAID, but also listed as myRAID under /proc. Note that this will only apply to RAIDs configured after the change to the configuration file. Active RAIDs will continue to use the mdN names until they get stopped and reassembled.

warning.title: Incompatible tools
warning.para: Not all tools may support named RAID devices. If a tool expects a RAID device to be named mdN, it will fail to identify the devices.

section.title: Configuring software RAID for the root partition
section.para: Setting up a software RAID 1 array for the root partition in &productname; 16 via the command line requires strict adherence to execution order. Executing these steps out of order will result in an unbootable system or data loss.

This procedure configures a software RAID 1 root partition on a &productname; 16 UEFI system and assumes two identical raw disks, /dev/sda and /dev/sdb , using a GPT partition scheme with a small BIOS Boot Partition (EF02) to allow GRUB2 embedding without requiring UEFI.

itemizedlist.title: Prerequisites for using a software RAID device for the root partition

listitem.para: You need two hard disks to create the RAID 1 mirror device. The hard disks should be similarly sized. The RAID assumes the size of the smaller drive. The block storage devices can be any combination of local (in or directly attached to the machine), Fibre Channel storage subsystems, or iSCSI storage subsystems.
A separate partition for /boot is not required if you install the boot loader in the MBR. If installing the boot loader in the MBR is not an option, /boot needs to reside on a separate partition.

For UEFI machines, you need to set up a dedicated /boot/efi partition. It needs to be VFAT-formatted, and may reside on the RAID 1 device to prevent booting problems in case the physical disk with /boot/efi fails.
If you are using hardware RAID devices, do not attempt to run software RAIDs on top of it.
If you are using iSCSI target devices, you need to enable the iSCSI initiator support before you create the RAID device.

If your storage subsystem provides multiple I/O paths between the server and its directly attached local devices, Fibre Channel devices, or iSCSI devices that you want to use in the software RAID, you need to enable the multipath support before you create the RAID device.
